Objective: This exercise serves the purpose of helping student using simple linear regression models.

  1. Find the number of observations (N), mean, standard deviation,min, quartiles and max for all numerical/integer variables: age, bmi,children, charges, and the dummy variables created in question 1. Save it as a data frame called summary_statistics.
summary_statistics <- medical_dataset %>%
  select(age, bmi, children, charges, starts_with("sex"),
         starts_with("smoker"), starts_with("region")) %>%
  summarise(list(
    Q1 = ~quantile(., 0.25),
    Median = ~median(.),
    Q3 = ~quantile(., 0.75),
    Max = ~max(.),
    N = ~length(.),
    Mean = ~mean(.),
    SD = ~sd(.),
    Min = ~min(.)
  ))

  1. Split the medical_data into training and test data sets with a 70-30 split and save them as train_strat and test_strat. Set your seed as 123. When split the data, please make sure each data set have the same proportion of smoker versus non-smoker. Run a simple linear regression model using train_strat and save it as “model_SL” and summary the output.

\[ charges = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times bmi + \varepsilon \]

library(caret)

set.seed(123)

train_index <- createDataPartition(medical_data$smoker,
                                   p = 0.7,
                                   list = FALSE)

train_strat <- medical_data[train_index, ]
test_strat  <- medical_data[-train_index, ]

model_SL <- lm(charges ~ bmi, data = train_strat)
summary(model_SL)

  1. To test the hypothesis that medical insurance charges is positively associated with policyholder’s bmi. Can you justify whether the training data support his hypothesis and why.

The training module doesn’t justify the null hypothesis, as the p value is extremely low. THis means that the values are corelated in some way.

  1. Find the confidence interval for model parameters at 95% confidence level. (\(\hat{\beta_1} \pm 2*SE\))
confint(model_SL, level = 0.95)
                 2.5 %   97.5 %
(Intercept) -2295.5624 5639.258
bmi           247.3604  500.127
  1. Check the histogram of residuals, and how to you evaluate your data.
residuals_SL <- residuals(model_SL)

hist(residuals_SL,
     main = "Histogram of Residuals",
     xlab = "Residuals")

Based on this Residual plot, the model shows that the residual plot is a bell curve, however the residual plot has a positive skew. There does not appear to be any outliers.

  1. Predict expected charges add it to train_strat and test_strat, and find mean squared errors, respectively
train_strat$predicted <- predict(model_SL, train_strat)

test_strat$predicted <- predict(model_SL, test_strat)

mse_train <- mean((train_strat$charges - train_strat$predicted)^2)
mse_test  <- mean((test_strat$charges - test_strat$predicted)^2)
